mainTopic: Rental disputes, the limits of borrowed items, and replacing a rented house that fell
overview: The amud opens by asking whether a landlord owed rent can swear and collect like a hired worker (שכיר). The גמרא says no: the worker's oath exists only because an employer is busy with many workers, so in a rent dispute the renter is believed with an oath. Next, רב נחמן rules that a landlord who rented out a house for ten years with a document is believed when he says five years are already used up. רבינא explains why this differs from a loan document: a rental document only protects the owner from a false ownership claim, while a loan document exists for collecting. Then come rules about borrowing items. Someone who borrows an item 'בטובו' may keep re-borrowing it while it works, but only with a קנין, and when it breaks he returns the handle. The borrower's exact wording ('this orchard', 'an orchard', 'orchards'; 'this well', 'a well', 'a place for a well') sets the limits of the loan. A new משנה rules that a landlord whose rented house fell must replace it with a matching house. After two attempts, the גמרא explains, following רבין's report of ריש לקיש, that the landlord said 'a house like this' about a riverbank house. The chapter השואל then closes, and the next chapter opens with a משנה about farming another person's field according to local custom, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Comparing the landlord to a hired worker
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that a landlord claiming unpaid rent should be like a שכיר, who swears and collects his wages.
steps.simpleTranslation: A hired worker who claims his pay on time takes an oath and collects it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up the rule of a hired worker to suggest that a landlord should also be able to swear and collect his rent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually an oath is used to avoid paying, not to collect. A שכיר is an exception, since he swears and then collects. The suggestion is that a landlord should get the same treatment, which pushes against the idea that the renter is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: At its proper time, on the day the wages are due

phrases.english: A hired worker who claims his pay at the proper time,
takes an oath and collects.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier position that the renter is believed when he claims he already paid
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the renter is believed when he says he paid the rent
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A שכיר swears and collects, so a landlord owed rent should also swear and collect.

steps.title: The worker's oath is a special case
steps.stepSummary: The rabbis gave the שכיר an oath only because an employer is busy with many workers. A renter has no such issue, so the renter is believed with an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is only a hired worker on whom the rabbis placed an oath, because an employer is busy with his workers. But here, the renter is believed with an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the comparison. The worker's rule was made for a special reason that does not apply to rent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An employer with many workers can easily mix up whom he paid, so the rabbis let the worker swear and collect. A renter deals with one landlord, so that worry is missing. The normal rule stays in place: the person being asked to pay (the renter) swears and is free.

keyTerms.meaning: The rabbis placed (an oath) upon him

steps.whatToRemember: The שכיר's right to swear and collect is a special rabbinic rule based on the employer being busy. It does not extend to rent, where the renter swears and is believed.

phrases.aramaic: שָׂכִיר הוּא דִּרְמוֹ רַבָּנַן שְׁבוּעָה עֲלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: It is specifically a hired worker on whom the rabbis placed an oath,
because the employer is busy with his workers.
But here, with rent,
the renter is believed with an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׂכִיר הוּא דִּרְמוֹ רַבָּנַן שְׁבוּעָה עֲלֵיהּ
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between a landlord and a hired worker
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The worker's oath depends on the employer being busy with many workers, and that reason does not apply to a landlord and renter.

steps.title: The landlord is believed that five years were used
steps.stepSummary: רבא quoting רב נחמן: a landlord who rented out a house for ten years with a document is believed when he says the renter already used five years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: Someone rented out a house to his friend for ten years and wrote him a document. If the landlord later says, 'You already used five years,' he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new rule begins. The landlord's claim that half the rental time is used up is accepted, even though the renter holds a ten-year document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might expect the renter's document to prove he still has the full ten years. רב נחמן rules that it does not, and the landlord is believed. The reason comes out in step 5.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Nachman said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דְּאוֹגַר לֵיהּ בֵּיתָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
phrases.english: Someone who rented out a house to his friend
for ten years, and wrote him a document,
and later said to him: You have already used five years,
phrases.notes: The landlord is the one speaking to the renter here.

phrases.english: he is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new rental ruling, this time about time used up rather than rent paid
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A landlord is believed when he claims the renter already used five of the ten rental years, despite the rental document.

steps.title: Challenge from a loan document
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי asks רבינא: by this logic, a borrower with a document who claims he repaid half should also be believed, which is not true.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדפתי said to רבינא: If so, if someone lent a hundred זוז with a document and the borrower says, 'I paid you back half,' should he also be believed?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא challenges רב נחמן's rule by comparing it to a loan. Everyone agrees the borrower is not believed in that case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases, someone claims that half of what the document records is already finished. If the landlord is believed against the rental document, the borrower should be believed against the loan document. Since he is not, the challenge is why rent should be different.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, אוֹזְפֵיהּ מְאָה זוּזֵי בִּשְׁטָרָא,
phrases.english: If so, if someone lent another a hundred zuz with a document,
and the borrower said to him: I paid you back half,
would he also be believed?
phrases.notes: This is a question meant to show a problem. Everyone agrees the borrower is not believed here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's ruling in step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that the landlord is believed against the rental document
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A borrower who claims partial repayment is not believed against a loan document. That case looks the same, so the landlord should not be believed either.

steps.title: A loan document and a rental document have different purposes
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains that a loan document exists to collect money, so any repayment should have been written down. A rental document only protects the owner from a false ownership claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: How can you compare them? There, the document exists for collecting. If he really paid, the lender should have written it on the back, or written a receipt. But here, the landlord can say: I wrote you the document only so you could not claim ownership of the house by living in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge by showing why the two documents are not alike.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan document is a tool for collecting. If part was really repaid, the borrower should have insisted on a note on the back or a receipt, so his word alone is weak. A rental document was never meant to record how many years are left. Its job is to stop the renter from claiming, after living there for years, that he owns the house. So it proves nothing against the landlord's claim about time used.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? (rejects a comparison)

steps.whatToRemember: What a document proves depends on why it was written. A loan document backs up the lender's right to collect. A rental document only protects the owner's ownership, so the landlord is believed about how much time was used.
steps.confusionAlert: The rental document is not useless. It does protect the landlord, but it does not help the renter prove how many years remain.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a broad principle: a document is judged by its purpose, and it cannot be used as evidence for something it was never written to prove.

phrases.english: He said to him: How can you compare them?!
There, the document exists for collecting,
so if it were true that he repaid him,
the lender should have written it on the back of the document,
or else written a receipt for it.
But here, the landlord can say to him:
The reason I wrote you a document
was so that you would not claim ownership of the house by living in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא's challenge in step 4 and defends רב נחמן's ruling
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by the purpose of each document
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both documents look alike, so a claim of partial completion should be treated the same in both cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: A loan document exists for collection, so any repayment should have been recorded. A rental document only guards against a false ownership claim, so the landlord is believed about the years used.

steps.title: Borrowing an item for as long as it is in good condition
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that a person may borrow an item 'בטובו', for as long as it stays in good working order, and this right lasts indefinitely.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: A person can borrow an item 'in its good condition' forever.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a statement from רב נחמן about a special kind of loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower asked to borrow the item for as long as it works well, the loan does not end when he gives it back once. He can keep taking it and using it again, and the owner cannot stop him, as long as the item is still in good condition.

keyTerms.meaning: In its good condition, for as long as it works well

steps.confusionAlert: 'Forever' does not mean the borrower never gives it back. It means that even after returning it, he may keep borrowing it again and again while it is still in good condition.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said:
A person may borrow [an item] in its good condition forever.
phrases.notes: He means: if he asked to borrow it 'for as long as it works', he can keep borrowing it again even after giving it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: שׁוֹאֵל אָדָם בְּטוּבוֹ לְעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, moving from rental disputes to the rules of a borrowing arrangement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who borrows an item 'בטובו' may keep using and re-borrowing it for as long as it stays in good working order.

steps.title: This only works if the borrower made a formal acquisition
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דבת שמואל limits רב נחמן's rule to a case where the borrower made a קנין with the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, the son of שמואל's daughter, said: And this is only when he made a קנין with him.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא adds a condition to רב נחמן's rule and narrows it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A simple request is not enough to lock the owner into an endless loan. Only if the borrower made a קנין, a formal act that makes the deal binding, does the right to keep re-borrowing hold. Without a קנין, once he returns the item he needs the owner's permission again.

keyTerms.meaning: A formal act that makes an agreement legally binding
He made a קנין with him
Son of שמואל's daughter, which identifies which רב מרי this is

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרַהּ דְּבַת שְׁמוּאֵל,
phrases.english: Rav Mari, son of the daughter of Shmuel, said:
And that is when he made an act of acquisition with him.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the corrected wording is in square brackets. Either way, he made a קנין with the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרַהּ דְּבַת שְׁמוּאֵל, וְהוּא דִּקְנוֹ מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting condition to רב נחמן's rule in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The endless 'בטובו' loan applies only when the borrower made a קנין with the owner.

steps.title: When the item breaks, the handle goes back to the owner
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב אשי adds that once the borrowed item breaks, the borrower must return its handle to the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, the son of רב אשי, said: And he must return its handle to him.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא adds a further detail to the 'בטובו' loan: what happens when the item stops being in good condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The loan was only for as long as the item is 'good'. Once it breaks, the loan is over, so the borrower cannot keep the broken parts. He must give back what is left, like the handle.

keyTerms.meaning: Its handle, the leftover parts of the broken tool

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Mari, son of Rav Ashi, said:
And he returns its handle to him.
phrases.notes: This is about when the tool breaks. Whatever is left of it, like the handle, goes back to the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אָשֵׁי: וּמַהְדַּר לֵיהּ קַתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another detail to the 'בטובו' rule of step 6: what happens when the item breaks.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the borrowed item breaks, the borrower must return its remaining parts (the handle) to the owner.

steps.title: The borrower's exact words set the limits of the loan
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that borrowing a hoe for 'this orchard' covers only that one orchard, 'an orchard' covers any one orchard, and 'orchards' covers all his orchards. In every case, the handle goes back when the hoe breaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone tells his friend, 'Lend me a hoe to dig this orchard', he may dig only that orchard. If he said 'an orchard', he may dig any one orchard he wants. If he said 'orchards', he may go on digging all the orchards he has. And he must return its handle to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new rule showing that the borrower's exact wording decides how much he may use the borrowed tool.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three levels. 'This orchard' points to one specific orchard. 'An orchard' lets him pick any single orchard. 'Orchards' (plural) lets him use the hoe in all his orchards, however many there are. רבא's closing line about returning the handle uses the same words as step 8 and applies that rule to all three cases.

keyTerms.meaning: To dig up or loosen the soil

steps.whatToRemember: A 'בטובו' loan lasts as long as the item works, but only with a קנין. When it breaks, the leftovers go back to the owner. The borrower's exact words ('this', 'an', or plural) set the limits of the loan.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general principle in loans: how far the borrower's rights reach depends on the precise words he used when he asked to borrow.

phrases.english: Rava said:
One who says to his friend:
'Lend me a hoe
to dig up this orchard with it' –
he may dig that orchard with it.
[If he said] 'an orchard' –
phrases.notes: Here he left out the word 'this', so he did not name any specific orchard.

phrases.english: he may dig with it any orchard he wants.
[If he said] 'orchards' –

phrases.aramaic: רָפֵיק וְאָזֵיל כֹּל פַּרְדֵּיסֵי דְּאִית לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: he may keep on digging all the orchards that he has,
and he returns its handle to him.
phrases.notes: These are the same words we saw in step 8. If the hoe breaks, the leftover handle goes back to the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: אוֹשְׁלַן מָרָא לְמִירְפַּק בֵּיהּ הַאי פַּרְדֵּיסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the borrowing topic with a new rule about the scope of a loan, and ends with the same 'return the handle' wording seen in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The scope of a borrowed tool's use follows the borrower's wording: 'this orchard' means only that one, 'an orchard' means any one, and 'orchards' means all of them. When it breaks, the handle is returned.

steps.title: Borrowing 'this well', 'a well', or 'a place for a well'
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules on borrowing a well. 'This well' ends when it collapses. 'A well' may be rebuilt. 'A place for a well' allows digging again and again until one works, but only with a קנין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: If someone tells his friend, 'Lend me this well,' and it collapses, he may not rebuild it. If he said 'a well' and it collapses, he may rebuild it. If he said 'a place for a well,' he may keep digging several wells in the owner's land until he finds one that works. For that, he needs to make a קנין with the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives another borrowing rule with three levels of wording, this time about a well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exact words of the request decide how far the borrower's right reaches. 'This well' ties the loan to one well, so the loan ends when that well collapses. 'A well' lets him rebuild that well, and 'a place for a well' lets him keep digging, which is a lasting right that needs a קנין.

keyTerms.meaning: a well or pit used for irrigation
to make a קנין (formal act of acquisition) with him

steps.whatToRemember: The more open the wording, the wider the borrower's right. A right that never ends needs a קנין.
steps.whyThisMatters: It follows the same pattern as רבא's hoe rule and רב מרי's קנין rule from steps 7 and 9, now applied to land.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa says:
One who says to his friend:
"Lend me this well," and it fell in –
he may not rebuild it.
"A well," and it fell in –
he may rebuild it.
"A place for a well" –
he may keep digging several wells in his land
until he happens upon a good one,
and he needs to make a kinyan with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא, הַאי מַאן דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same three-level wording pattern from רבא's hoe rule to a borrowed well
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'This well' cannot be rebuilt. 'A well' can be rebuilt. 'A place for a well' allows digging until one works, but only with a קנין.

steps.title: A rented house that fell must be replaced with the same kind of house
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a landlord whose rented house collapsed must provide another house. The new house must match the old one in size, number of rooms, and windows, unless both sides agree to a change.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who rents a house to another, and it collapses, must provide him with a house. If it was small, he may not make it large. If it was large, he may not make it small. If it had one room, he may not make it two. If it had two rooms, he may not make it one. He may not reduce the number of windows or add to them, unless both of them agree.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It says a landlord must replace a rented house that fell, and the replacement must match the original.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The landlord's duty does not end when the building falls. He still owes the renter a house. However, he cannot change the house's size, rooms, or windows on his own, because either side might be harmed by the change. A change needs both of them to agree.

keyTerms.meaning: to provide him with a house
with the agreement of both of them

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who rents out a house to another, and it fell –
is obligated to provide him with a house.
If it was small, he may not make it large;
if large, he may not make it small.
If one, he may not make it two;
phrases.notes: 'One' and 'two' here mean the number of rooms.

phrases.english: if two, he may not make it one.
He may not reduce the windows
nor add to them,
except with the agreement of both of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: a landlord's duty when a rented house collapses
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The landlord must replace a fallen rented house with one of the same size, rooms, and windows, unless both agree otherwise.

steps.title: What kind of rental does the משנה mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה describes. If the landlord rented 'this house,' its collapse should end the deal. If he rented 'a house' with no details, he should be allowed to build any house at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the case? If he told him 'this house,' then once it fell, it is gone and there is nothing to replace. If he told him 'a house' with no details, then why can't he make one room into two, and why can't he make a small house into a large one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to picture the case in the משנה and shows that both possible readings run into a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires a replacement, but it also requires the replacement to match the original. 'This house' explains why it must match, but then no replacement should be owed at all. 'A house' explains why a replacement is owed, but then the landlord should be free to build any house. So neither reading explains both rules together.

keyTerms.meaning: the Talmudic discussion of the משנה
what is the case? how do we picture it?

steps.confusionAlert: This question is not attacking the משנה's ruling. It only shows that neither simple way of picturing the rental fits both parts of the משנה, and so a third case is needed.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
What are the circumstances?
If he said to him: "This house,"
it fell, it is gone.
If he said to him: "A house," without details,
why may he not make one into two,
why may he not make small into large!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״בַּיִת זֶה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how to picture the משנה's rental case
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that a replacement is owed and that it must match the original
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A specific house ends when it falls, so no replacement would be owed. An unspecified house allows any replacement, so it would not have to match. Neither case explains both rules.

steps.title: The landlord promised a house of stated measurements
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that the landlord said, 'The house I rent you is this long.' The deal was not for one particular building, so a replacement is owed. Its size was fixed, so the replacement must match.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: The case is where he told him, 'The house that I am renting to you has a length of such and such.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the question by describing a middle case between 'this house' and 'a house.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the landlord described a house by its measurements and did not name one building, his duty continues even after the building falls. Because he stated the measurements, the replacement has to be built to them. This explains both rules in the משנה at once.
steps.whatToRemember: This first answer explains why a replacement is owed and why it must match. Step 14 challenges it, and step 15 replaces it with רבין's version.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Where he said to him: "The house that I am renting to you,
the measure of its length is such and such."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by describing a third kind of rental
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case as a middle option between the two choices
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rental had to be either a specific house or a completely unspecified one, and neither fits the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rental was for a house of stated measurements. A replacement is owed, and it must match those measurements.

steps.title: If the size was stated, why teach it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's explanation: if the landlord stated the size, matching it is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the point of saying it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from Step 13. If the landlord said 'the house is this long,' of course the new house must match, so why does the משנה bother teaching it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 solved one problem: why a replacement is owed and why it must match. But this makes the משנה's ruling look too simple. A משנה is expected to teach something we would not have known.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is the case
Why say it? It is obvious

phrases.english: If so, what is there to say?
phrases.notes: He means: if the landlord spelled out the size, the משנה's ruling is too obvious to need teaching.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation of ריש לקיש given in Step 13 for being too obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's case of 'the house I rent you is this long'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the size was openly stated, a matching replacement is self-evident, so the משנה would teach nothing new.

steps.title: רבין's version: 'A house like this'
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports ריש לקיש's case differently: the landlord said, 'I am renting you a house like this.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רבין came, he said that ריש לקיש said: the landlord told him, 'I am renting you a house like this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא replaces the earlier version with the version רבין brought: the landlord said 'a house like this,' pointing at a house, instead of stating a length.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deal is still not for one specific building, so a replacement is owed. But now the size is described by comparison ('like this') instead of exact measurements, which opens a question about what 'like this' covers.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)

phrases.english: Rather, when Ravin came,
he said that Reish Lakish said:
It is where he said to him:
'I am renting you a house like this.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 14 by bringing a different report of ריש לקיש's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case through a different report
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case was an exact stated length, which made the ruling obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is 'a house like this,' a comparison rather than a stated measurement.

steps.title: Still obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks again: even with 'a house like this,' the ruling seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: And still, what is the point of saying it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is not satisfied. If the landlord said 'a house like this,' clearly the new house must be like it, so why teach it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Changing the wording to 'like this' still seems to point plainly to the same size and layout. The גמרא wants to find what the משנה is truly adding.

phrases.english: And still, what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the 'obvious' challenge against רבין's version.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Like this' plainly means a similar house, so the משנה's matching rule still seems self-evident.

steps.title: The house was on a riverbank
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed where the model house stood on a riverbank; 'like this' refers to the house itself, not its riverbank location.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where the house stood on a riverbank. You might have said: what does 'like this' mean? A house standing on a riverbank. So the משנה teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה is needed for a special case: the house the landlord pointed to stood on a riverbank. The משנה teaches that 'like this' means the same kind of house, not a house in the same kind of spot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the משנה, we might think 'like this' meant 'a house on a riverbank,' so the landlord would only need to give some riverbank house. The משנה's details (size, rooms, windows) show that 'like this' is about the building itself. That is the new lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case
On the bank of a river

steps.whatToRemember: The final explanation: the landlord said 'a house like this' about a riverbank house, and the משנה teaches that 'like this' means the same size and layout, not the same location.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary:
where it stood on the bank of a river.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the house the landlord pointed to when he said 'like this.'

phrases.english: You might have said:
what is 'like this'?
one that stands on the bank of a river,
so it teaches us.
phrases.notes: It teaches that 'like this' means a house of the same size and layout.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 16 by finding a case where the משנה's ruling is not obvious.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to show a new lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Like this' might mean a house in a similar spot, on a riverbank.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Like this' refers to the house's size and structure, as the משנה details.

steps.title: הדרן — Closing פרק השואל
steps.stepSummary: The closing line for the chapter called השואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, השואל.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the chapter called השואל, about borrowing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן is a traditional farewell said at the end of each chapter, promising to come back and learn it again. It is not part of the legal discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (closing a chapter)
The borrower; the name of the chapter

phrases.english: We will return to you, HaSho'el.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter after the last discussion ended in Step 17.

steps.title: Farming another's field follows local custom
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה teaches that one who takes on another's field to farm follows local custom in harvesting and plowing, and the two sides split by-products just as they split the main crop.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who takes a field from his fellow to farm: where people are used to cutting the crop, he must cut; to uprooting, he must uproot; to plowing after harvest, he must plow. Everything follows the custom of the region. Just as they split the grain, so they split the stubble and the straw. Just as they split the wine, so they split...
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter opens with a משנה about a person who takes over someone's field to farm it. The משנה says he must work it the way people locally do, and that the owner and farmer share the leftovers too, not only the main crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: How to harvest (cutting or uprooting) and whether to plow afterward matter to the owner, since they affect the field. The משנה makes local custom the rule. It also adds that sharing extends to by-products like stubble and straw. The text continues on the next lines with what is split alongside the wine.

keyTerms.meaning: One who takes on a field to farm it
To uproot (the crop with its roots)

steps.confusionAlert: The word מקבל here does not mean 'one who receives a gift.' It means someone who takes on another person's field to work it, paying the owner with part of the crop.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the theme of the new chapter: working another's field, where local custom shapes what each side owes.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who takes a field from his fellow,
phrases.notes: He takes it to farm, paying the owner with a share or a set amount of the crop.

phrases.english: a place where they are used to cutting —
he must cut;

to plowing after it — he must plow;

Just as they divide the grain,

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A farmer of another's field must harvest and plow according to local custom, and the by-products are shared just like the main crop.
